title: OpenAI is adding an invisible watermark to AI-generated text
key_facts: OpenAI is adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex, its programming agent, so machines can identify it as AI-written.
The change is mandatory in the EU and opt-in for API customers elsewhere, on select models, where it is off by default; the EU rollout across ChatGPT and Codex takes place over the next few weeks.
The system, called textGrain, changes how the model picks words using pseudorandom values from a secret key, leaving a statistical signal that detectors can test for.
OpenAI's detection tool is limited to researchers and experts who apply for access; in tests it caught the watermark in 80 percent of 200-word AI passages.

Changing 10 percent of the words in a 400-word passage cut detection to 66 percent, and replacing 25 percent cut it to 17 percent; detection is also weaker on topics with rigid vocabulary such as mathematics.
OpenAI says a watermark cannot establish ownership, prove accuracy or identify who wrote the prompt, and that a missing watermark does not prove a human wrote the text.
The step responds to Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act; providers whose models were released before 2 Aug have until 2 Dec to comply or face fines of up to three percent of worldwide annual turnover.
Mashable says Anthropic announced earlier this year that Claude would watermark its output worldwide.
quote_evidence: OpenAI is adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and programming agent Codex, making it easier for machines to identify that it was written by AI.
In testing, the tool only caught watermarks in 80 percent of 200-word AI-generated passages, with detection rates even lower when said text was on topics with rigid lexicons such as mathematics.
"Text watermarking and detection remain early technologies with significant limitations, and views about their benefits and responsible uses are still developing," OpenAI said in its announcement.
why_it_matters_hint: A big chatbot maker will mark its text to meet EU law, but its own tests show light editing can erase the mark.
event_date: Announced 11-12 Oct 2026 (Mashable's Australia-based writer says 'Monday'; the pool timestamp is Sunday 11 Oct 15:05 UTC); EU compliance deadline 2 Dec 2026
notes: Official OpenAI announcement as relayed by Mashable. Mashable discloses that its parent Ziff Davis sued OpenAI in April 2025 over copyright.
